o: Removing elements so the rest is non-decreasing is equivalent to keeping a maximum-size non-decreasing subsequence — here values are only 1, 2, 3. Since there are just three values, we can track the longest non-decreasing subsequence length with three counters: c1 = longest kept suffix of 1s, c2 = longest kept sequence of 1s then 2s, c3 = 1s then 2s then 3s. Answer = n − max(c1, c2, c3). Example 1: [2,1,3,2,1] keeps e.g. [1,2] or [1,1] (length 2), removing 3. Example 3 needs 0 removals.
k: Minimum deletions = n − length of the longest non-decreasing subsequence.
With only 3 distinct values, the LIS-style DP collapses to three scalar counters updated in O(1) per element.

a.i: Process elements left to right. Seeing a 1 extends c1; seeing a 2 extends max(c1,c2)+1; seeing a 3 extends max(c1,c2,c3)+1. The best of the three counters is the longest non-decreasing subsequence.
s: For each value: 1 → c1++; 2 → c2 = max(c2, c1) + 1; 3 → c3 = max(c3, c1, c2) + 1.

a.i: Treat it as longest non-decreasing subsequence: dp[i] = longest valid subsequence ending at i, computed in O(n²) by scanning predecessors. Works for arbitrary alphabets and easily fits n ≤ 100.
s: For j < i with nums[j] ≤ nums[i], dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j]+1).

w: Prefer the O(n) counter DP; it directly answers the follow-up. Pitfall: 'non-decreasing' allows equal values, so comparisons are ≤, not <. Another equivalent view: min deletions to reach one of the patterns 1…12…23…3, solvable with prefix/suffix counts. Test with reverse-sorted input (answer n−1) and constant arrays (answer 0).
